source_text: Θυσία δὲ ἡ τῷ θεῷ δεκτὴ σώματός τε καὶ τῶν τούτου παθῶν ἀμετανόητος χωρισμός. ἡ ἀληθὴς τῷ ὄντι θεοσέβεια αὕτη. καὶ μή τι εἰκότως μελέτη θανάτου διὰ τοῦτο εἴρηται τῷ Σωκράτει ἡ φιλοσοφία· ὁ γὰρ μήτε τὴν ὄψιν παρατιθέμενος ἐν τῷ διανοεῖσθαι μήτε τινὰ τῶν ἄλλων αἰσθήσεων ἐφελκόμενος, ἀλλ’ αὐτῷ καθαρῷ τῷ νῷ τοῖς πράγμασιν ἐντυγχάνων τὴν ἀληθῆ φιλοσοφίαν μέτεισιν. τοῦτο ἄρα βούλεται καὶ τῷ Πυθαγόρᾳ ἡ τῆς πενταετίας σιωπή, ἣν τοῖς γνωρίμοις παρεγγυᾷ, ὡς δὴ ἀποστραφέντες τῶν αἰσθητῶν ψιλῷ τῷ νῷ τὸ θεῖον ἐποπτεύοιεν. παρὰ Μωυσέως τοιαῦτα φιλοσοφήσαντες οἱ τῶν Ἑλλήνων ἄκροι. προστάσσει γὰρ τὰ ὁλοκαυτώματα δείραντας εἰς μέλη διανεῖμαι, ἐπειδὴ γυμνὴν τῆς ὑλικῆς δορᾶς γενομένην τὴν γνωστικὴν ψυχὴν ἄνευ τῆς σωματικῆς φλυαρίας καὶ τῶν παθῶν πάντων, ὅσα περιποιοῦσιν αἱ κεναὶ καὶ ψευδεῖς ὑπολήψεις, ἀποδυσαμένην τὰς σαρκικὰς ἐπιθυμίας, τῷ φωτὶ καθιερωθῆναι ἀνάγκη. οἱ δὲ πλεῖστοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸ θνητὸν ἐνδυόμενοι καθάπερ οἱ κοχλίαι καὶ περὶ τὰς αὑτῶν ἀκρασίας ὥσπερ οἱ ἐχῖνοι σφαιρηδὸν εἱλούμενοι περὶ τοῦ μακαρίου καὶ ἀφθάρτου θεοῦ τοιαῦτα οἷα καὶ περὶ αὑτῶν δοξάζουσιν. λέληθεν δ’ αὐτούς, κἂν πλησίον ἡμῶν τύχωσιν, ὡς μυρία ὅσα δεδώρηται ἡμῖν ὁ θεός, ὧν αὐτὸς ἀμέτοχος, γένεσιν μὲν ἀγένητος ὤν, τροφὴν δὲ ἀνενδεὴς ὤν, καὶ αὔξησιν ἐν ἰσότητι ὤν, εὐγηρίαν τε καὶ εὐθανασίαν ἀθάνατός τε καὶ ἀγήρως ὑπάρχων. διὸ καὶ χεῖρας καὶ πόδας καὶ στόμα καὶ ὀφθαλμοὺς καὶ εἰσόδους καὶ ἐξόδους καὶ ὀργὰς καὶ ἀπειλὰς μὴ πάθη θεοῦ τις ὑπολάβῃ παρὰ Ἑβραίοις λέγεσθαι, μηδαμῶς, ἀλληγορεῖσθαι δέ τινα ἐκ τούτων τῶν ὀνομάτων ὁσιώτερον, ἃ δὴ καὶ προϊόντος τοῦ λόγου κατὰ τὸν οἰκεῖον καιρὸν διασαφήσομεν. ἦ πανακὲς πάντων φάρμακον ἁ σοφία, Καλλίμαχος ἐν τοῖς ἐπιγράμμασι γράφει· ἕτερος (δὲ) ἐξ ἑτέρου σοφὸς τό τε πάλαι τό τε νῦν, φησὶ Βακχυλίδης ἐν τοῖς Παιᾶσιν· οὐδὲ γὰρ ῥᾷστον ἀρρήτων ἐπέων πύλας ἐξευρεῖν· καλῶς ἄρα Ἰσοκράτης ἐν τῷ Παναθηναϊκῷ τίνας οὖν καλῶ πεπαιδευμένους; προθεὶς ἐπιφέρει· πρῶτον μὲν τοὺς καλῶς χρωμένους τοῖς πράγμασι τοῖς κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν ἑκάστην προσπίπτουσι καὶ τὴν δόξαν ἐπιτυχῆ τῶν καιρῶν ἔχοντας καὶ δυναμένην ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ στοχάζεσθαι τοῦ συμφέροντος· ἔπειτα τοὺς πρεπόντως καὶ δικαίως ὁμιλοῦντας ἀεὶ τοῖς πλησιάζουσι καὶ τὰς μὲν τῶν ἄλλων ἀηδίας καὶ βαρύτητας εὐκόλως καὶ ῥᾳδίως φέροντας, σφᾶς δ’ αὐτοὺς ὡς δυνατὸν ἐλαφροτάτους καὶ μετριωτάτους τοῖς ξυνοῦσι παρέχοντας· ἔτι δὲ τοὺς τῶν μὲν ἡδονῶν κρατοῦντας, τῶν δὲ συμφορῶν μὴ λίαν ἡττωμένους, ἀλλ’ ἀνδρωδῶς ἐν αὐταῖς ἀναστρεφομένους καὶ τῆς φύσεως ἀξίως ἧς μετέχοντες τυγχάνομεν· τέταρτον, ὅπερ μέγιστόν ἐστι, τοὺς μὴ διαφθειρομένους ὑπὸ τῶν εὐπραγιῶν μηδ’ ἐξισταμένους αὑτῶν μηδὲ ὑπερηφάνους γινομένους, ἀλλ’ ἐμμένοντας τῇ τάξει τῶν εὖ φρονούντων. εἶτα ἐπιφέρει τὸν κολοφῶνα τοῦ λόγου· τοὺς δὲ μὴ μόνον πρὸς ἓν τούτων, ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἅπαντα ταῦτα τὴν ἕξιν τῆς ψυχῆς εὐάρμοστον ἔχοντας, τούτους φημὶ καὶ φρονίμους εἶναι καὶ τελείους ἄνδρας καὶ πάσας ἔχειν τὰς ἀρετάς. ὁρᾷς πῶς τὸν γνωστικὸν βίον καὶ Ἕλληνες, καίτοι μὴ εἰδότες ὡς ἐπίστασθαι χρή, ἐκθειάζουσι; τίς δ’ ἔστιν ἡ γνῶσις, οὐδὲ ὄναρ ἴσασιν. Εἰ τοίνυν λογικὸν ἡμῖν βρῶμα ἡ γνῶσις εἶναι συμπεφώνηται, μακάριοι τῷ ὄντι κατὰ τὴν γραφὴν οἱ πεινῶντες καὶ διψῶντες τὴν ἀλήθειαν, ὅτι πλησθήσονται τροφῆς ἀιδίου. πάνυ θαυμαστῶς ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς σκηνῆς φιλόσοφος Εὐριπίδης τοῖς προειρημένοις ἡμῖν συνῳδὸς διὰ τούτων εὑρίσκεται, πατέρα καὶ υἱὸν ἅμα οὐκ οἶδ’ ὅπως αἰνισσόμενος· σοὶ τῷ πάντων μεδέοντι χοὴν πέλανόν τε φέρω, Ζεὺς εἴτ’ Ἀίδης ὀνομαζόμενος στέργεις· σὺ δέ μοι θυσίαν ἄπυρον παγκαρπείας δέξαι πλήρη προχυτίαν. ὁλοκάρπωμα γὰρ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἄπυρον θῦμα ὁ Χριστός. καὶ ὅτι τὸν σωτῆρα αὐτὸν οὐκ εἰδὼς λέγει, σαφὲς ποιήσει ἐπάγων· σὺ γὰρ ἔν τε θεοῖς τοῖς οὐρανίδαις σκῆπτρον τὸ Διὸς μεταχειρίζεις χθονίων τ’ Ἀίδῃ μετέχεις ἀρχῆς. ἔπειτα ἄντικρυς λέγει· πέμψον δ’ ἐς φῶς ψυχὰς ἐνέρων τοῖς βουλομένοις ἄθλους προμαθεῖν πόθεν ἔβλαστον, τίς ῥίζα κακῶν, τίνα δεῖ μακάρων ἐκθυσαμένους εὑρεῖν μοχθῶν ἀνάπαυλαν. οὐκ ἀπεικότως ἄρα καὶ τῶν μυστηρίων τῶν παρ’ Ἕλλησιν ἄρχει μὲν τὰ καθάρσια, καθάπερ καὶ τοῖς βαρβάροις τὸ λουτρόν. μετὰ ταῦτα δ’ ἐστὶ τὰ μικρὰ μυστήρια διδασκαλίας τινὰ ὑπόθεσιν ἔχοντα καὶ προπαρασκευῆς τῶν μελλόντων, τὰ δὲ μεγάλα περὶ τῶν συμπάντων, οὗ μανθάνειν οὐκέτι ὑπολείπεται, ἐποπτεύειν δὲ καὶ περινοεῖν τήν τε φύσιν καὶ τὰ πράγματα.
pass_a_gloss: The sacrifice acceptable to God is the separation from the body and its passions without regret. This is true reverence for the existing God. And it is not without reason that the study of death is called philosophy by Socrates; for he who neither presents sight in his thinking nor is drawn to any of the other senses, but encounters things with his pure mind, pursues true philosophy. This is also what Pythagoras intends with his five-year silence, which he prescribes for those familiar with him, so that, turning away from sensory things, they may contemplate the divine with a pure mind. The greatest of the Greeks have philosophized in this way, following Moses. For he commands that the whole burnt offerings, having been flayed, be divided into parts, since the knowing soul, having become naked of the material skin and having put off the bodily chatter and all the passions, which the empty and false assumptions produce, and having stripped off the fleshly desires, must be consecrated to the light. But most people, putting on the mortal, like snails and being curled up around their own excesses like hedgehogs, think such things about the blessed and immortal God as they also think about themselves. It has escaped their notice, even if they are near us, how many things God has given us, of which He Himself is without share, being unborn, without need of nourishment, and equal in growth, and having a good old age and a good death, being immortal and ageless. Therefore, no one should suppose that hands or feet or mouth or eyes or entrances or exits or organs or threats are passions of God, as is said among the Hebrews; rather, it is more proper to allegorize some of these names. Wisdom is the panacea of all things, as Callimachus writes in his epigrams; another wise man comes from another, both in the past and in the present, as Bacchylides says in his Paeans; for it is not easy to find the gates of unutterable words. Isocrates says well in his Panathenaic Oration, 'What kind of men, then, do I call educated?' He proposes and adds, 'First, those who use things well, which happen every day, and have a good reputation in their times and are able to think about what is advantageous for the most part; then, those who converse properly and justly with those who approach them and bear the unpleasantness and heaviness of others easily and lightly, while presenting themselves as light and moderate as possible to those who are with them; and also those who master their pleasures and are not overly defeated by their misfortunes, but live bravely in them and worthily of the nature in which we share; and fourth, which is the greatest, those who are not corrupted by their good fortune nor become arrogant, but remain in the order of those who think well.' Then he adds the conclusion of his speech, 'But I say that those who have a disposition of the soul that is well-fitted not just for one of these things, but for all of them, are wise and perfect men and have all the virtues.' Do you see how the Greeks, although they do not know how to know, praise the knowing life? What is knowledge, they do not even dream. If, then, it has been agreed that knowledge is our rational food, blessed are those who hunger and thirst for truth, for they will be filled with eternal food. The philosopher Euripides, on the stage, is found to be in harmony with what has been said, not knowing how to praise the Father and the Son at the same time; 'I bring you a bowl and a cup, Zeus, whether you are called Hades or not; accept from me a sacrifice of full and complete abundance, without fire.' For Christ is a whole burnt offering, a sacrifice without fire, on our behalf. And that he is speaking about the Savior without knowing it, he will make clear by adding, 'For you wield the scepter of Zeus among the heavenly gods and share the rule of Hades among the earthly gods.' Then he says straightforwardly, 'Send into the light the souls of those who wish to learn about contests, from what source I sprang, what is the root of evils, what kind of blessed things one must seek, having sacrificed and found rest from labors.' It is not without reason, then, that the mysteries of the Greeks also begin with purifications, just like the bath among the barbarians. After these are the minor mysteries, which have some teaching and preparation for what is to come, and the greater mysteries are about all things, where there is no longer anything to learn, but only to contemplate and think about nature and things.
pass_b_english: The sacrifice that God accepts is separation from the body and its passions without regret; this is true reverence for the living God. It is no coincidence that Socrates calls philosophy a study of death: one who neither brings sight into his thinking nor lets any other sense draw him away, but meets reality with a pure mind, attains true philosophy. Pythagoras aims at the same end with the five-year silence he prescribes for his disciples, so that, turning from sensory things, they may contemplate the divine with a bare mind. The greatest Greek thinkers have philosophized in this way, following Moses. He commands that whole burnt offerings be flayed and divided into parts, because the knowing soul, stripped of its material skin, must put off bodily chatter and all the passions that empty, false assumptions produce, strip away fleshly desires, and be consecrated to the light. Most people, however, clothe themselves in mortality like snails and curl around their own excesses like hedgehogs; they think of the blessed, immortal God exactly as they think of themselves. They fail to notice, even when they are near us, how many gifts God has given us — gifts of which He Himself has no share, since He is unborn, needs no nourishment, remains equal in growth, enjoys a good old age and a good death, and is immortal and ageless. Therefore no one should suppose that hands, feet, mouth, eyes, entrances, exits, organs, or threats are passions of God, as is said among the Hebrews; rather, it is more proper to allegorize some of these names, which we will clarify in due course as the discussion proceeds.

"Wisdom is the panacea for all things," Callimachus writes in his epigrams; "One wise man comes from another, both in the past and in the present," says Bacchylides in his Paeans, for the gates of unutterable words are not easily found. Isocrates speaks well in his Panathenaic Oration: "What kind of men, then, do I call educated?" He answers: first, those who use well the things that confront them each day, who have a good reputation in their times and can for the most part discern what is advantageous; second, those who converse properly and justly with those who approach them, who bear the unpleasantness and heaviness of others easily and lightly while presenting themselves as light and moderate as possible to their companions; third, those who master their pleasures and are not overly defeated by misfortunes, but live bravely in them and worthily of the nature we share; and fourth, which is greatest, those who are not corrupted by good fortune nor become arrogant, but remain in the order of those who think well. Then he adds the conclusion: "But I say that those who have a disposition of soul well-fitted not for just one of these things, but for all of them, are wise and perfect men and possess all the virtues." Do you see how the Greeks, though they do not know how to know, praise the knowing life? They do not even dream what knowledge is. If, then, it is agreed that knowledge is our rational food, blessed indeed are those who hunger and thirst for truth, for they will be filled with eternal food.

The philosopher Euripides, on the stage, is found to harmonize with what has been said, though he does not know how to praise Father and Son together: "I bring you a bowl and a cup, Zeus, whether you are called Hades or not; accept from me a sacrifice of full and complete abundance, without fire." For Christ is a whole burnt offering, a sacrifice without fire, on our behalf. That he speaks of the Savior without knowing it, he will make clear by adding: "For you wield the scepter of Zeus among the heavenly gods and share the rule of Hades among the earthly gods." Then he says plainly: "Send into the light the souls of those who wish to learn the contests, from what source I sprang, what is the root of evils, what kind of blessed things one must seek, having sacrificed and found rest from labors." It is not without reason, then, that the Greek mysteries also begin with purifications, just as the bath does among the barbarians. After these come the minor mysteries, which contain some teaching and preparation for what is to come; the greater mysteries concern all things, where nothing more remains to be learned, but only to contemplate and think through nature and reality.
